title: Hunting a Decay the Standard Model Forbids
hook: A tau lepton turning into a muon and a photon is essentially impossible in the Standard Model. Belle II looked hard and found nothing — which is exactly how you corner new physics.
key_points: Lepton flavour is conserved in the Standard Model, so tau to muon plus photon is effectively forbidden.
Many extensions of the Standard Model predict the decay at rates a search could reach.
Belle II searched 428 inverse femtobarns of electron-positron collision data from SuperKEKB.
A multivariate classifier suppressed Standard Model backgrounds before a likelihood fit extracted any signal.
No significant excess appeared, giving a branching-fraction limit below 9.5e-8 at 90% confidence.
Null results like this shrink the parameter space that new-physics models are allowed to occupy.
content_html: Leptons come in three families — electron, muon, tau — and in the Standard Model a particle does not simply hop between them. That rule, lepton flavour conservation, makes the decay of a tau into a muon plus a photon effectively forbidden. Which is precisely why experimentalists keep looking for it: a single confirmed event would be new physics, not a statistical fluctuation in a busy background.
extra_html:
The Belle II collaboration reported its latest search in August 2026, using 428 inverse femtobarns of electron-positron collision data from the SuperKEKB collider. The analysis trains a multivariate classifier to push down Standard Model processes that can fake the signature, then extracts any remaining signal with an extended maximum-likelihood fit.

No significant excess appeared. Using the CLs technique, the collaboration sets an upper limit on the branching fraction of 9.5 x 10^-8 at 90% confidence (12.2 x 10^-8 at 95%). That is the whole value of the exercise: many proposed extensions of the Standard Model — supersymmetry, leptoquarks, heavy neutral leptons — predict lepton-flavour violation at rates within reach of experiments like this one. Each tightening bound deletes a slice of their allowed parameter space, and the searches will continue as Belle II accumulates data.

related.title: The Sharpest Look Yet at the Tau's Tiny Magnet
related.hook: Every charged particle is a tiny magnet, and quantum jitters nudge its strength. Measuring that nudge tests the Standard Model — and CMS just made the best check yet for the tau lepton.

related.title: The Standard Model
related.hook: Almost everything around you is built from a handful of particles obeying three forces — and one theory predicts it all with jaw-dropping precision, yet still can't explain gravity.

related.title: Is the Muon Lopsided? Still No Sign of It
related.hook: A particle with a permanent electric dipole moment would violate time-reversal symmetry and point straight at new physics. Muon g-2 just squeezed the muon's limit tighter — and it stays at zero.

related.title: The muon puzzle: air showers make more muons than physics predicts
related.hook: Cosmic rays hitting the atmosphere produce far more muons than any collider-tuned model expects. Auger now says the fix is that proton collisions must dump several times more energy into hadrons.

flashcards.prompt: Why is the decay of a tau into a muon and a photon such a clean test for new physics?

choices.text: The Standard Model effectively forbids it, so any sighting would have to come from something new
It happens constantly, so its rate is easy to measure precisely
It is the only decay that produces a photon

flashcards.explanation_html: Lepton flavour conservation makes the rate negligible in the Standard Model. With essentially no expected signal, a detection could not be background.

flashcards.prompt: What does an upper limit on a branching fraction tell you when no signal is found?
flashcards.back_html: How rare the decay must be — here below 9.5e-8 at 90% confidence — which rules out any new-physics model predicting it more often than that.
